news.content: supreme courtgooglecbied E हिं অ বাং ગુ ಕ മ म ଓ ਪੰ த తె ار National English हिंदी उत्तर प्रदेशउत्तराखंडछत्तीसगढ़झारखंडदिल्लीबिहारमध्य प्रदेशराजस्थानहरियाणाहिमाचल प्रदेश অসমীয়া বাংলা ગુજરાતી ಕನ್ನಡ മലയാളം मराठी ଓଡିଆ ਪੰਜਾਬੀ தமிழ் తెలుగు ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్తెలంగాణ اردو Live NATIONAL WORLD SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT OPINION PHOTOS HEALTH STATE BUSINESS More Live ETV Bharat / bharat Nipah Drug Row Puts Keralam’s Public Health Record Under Scrutiny; Health Minister Faces Questions Expired Remdesivir suspicion triggers political row; ex-minister Veena George and doctors dispute any link to Nipah deaths; controversy puts state’s celebrated outbreak-management record under spotlight. Critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar has also challenged any suggestion of a causal link between Remdesivir and the six Nipah deaths cited in the controversy. (IANS) By ETV Bharat English Team Published : October 30, 2026 at 9:00 PM IST 5 Min Read Thiruvananthapuram: Kerala’s response to successive Nipah outbreaks, once held up as an example of public-health coordination, has become the focus of a political controversy after the government disclosed suspicions that potentially expired Remdesivir vials may have been administered to patients at Kozhikode Medical College between 2023 and 2025. The disclosure by Health Minister K Muraleedharan in the Legislative Assembly on Thursday has put the state’s healthcare administration under scrutiny and triggered a political confrontation between the ruling Congress-led United Democratic Front and the opposition led by Communist Part of India (Marxists) Left Democratic Front. It has also placed the minister on the defensive, with former Health Minister Veena George and medical professionals challenging the implications of his statement. The controversy is particularly sensitive because Kerala’s response to Nipah has received considerable national and international attention since the first outbreak in 2018. The question now is not merely whether expired medicine was used, but how such a possibility could arise in a public healthcare institution, whether patients were exposed to any risk and whether the state’s drug-supply and monitoring systems failed. Responding to a submission by Congress MLA representing Muvattupuzha Mathew Kuzhalnadan, Muraleedharan told the Assembly that records from Kozhikode Medical College had raised suspicions that Remdesivir vials with an expiry date of May 30, 2023, may have been used in subsequent years. The Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) had last purchased 3,000 vials of the drug through its Karunya scheme on June 3, 2021, at a cost of Rs 42 lakh. According to the minister, hospital records showed that 102 vials were used in 2023-24, 34 in 2024-25 and 10 in 2025-26. The 50 vials recorded as used in 2026-27 were reportedly brought from Bahrain on June 12, 2026, and administered to a Nipah patient who recovered. The government has ordered a detailed inquiry by a medical board headed by Dr R Aravind, head of the Department of Infectious Diseases at Thiruvananthapuram Medical College. The Directorate of Medical Education and the Directorate of Health Services have also been asked to trace patients who received the drug and examine whether its use had any adverse consequences. The inquiry is expected to establish whether the vials administered in the earlier years were indeed past their expiry dates, whether they were given to Nipah patients and whether there was any impact on treatment outcomes. Veena Dares Muraleedharan’s claim Former Health Minister Veena George of the CPI(M) has strongly disputed the implication that expired Remdesivir was administered to Nipah patients or contributed to their deaths. She has questioned the basis of the allegation and maintained that the patients who received the drug survived. The Congress-led UDF government disclosed suspicions that potentially expired Remdesivir vials may have been administered to patients at Kozhikode Medical College. (ETV Bharat) Critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar has also challenged any suggestion of a causal link between Remdesivir and the six Nipah deaths cited in the controversy. According to him, none of those patients received the drug at Kozhikode Medical College: Four died before Nipah was confirmed, while the other two were treated elsewhere. The competing claims have made the medical board’s findings crucial. The distinction between the number of vials recorded as consumed, the patients to whom they were administered and the actual expiry status of each batch will be central to determining whether there was a breach of medical protocol. Political Embarrassment For UDF The disclosure has created an uncomfortable situation for the UDF government. While the Health Minister has said the suspicion emerged from official records and ordered an investigation, the former LDF Health Minister’s rebuttal has challenged the political and medical implications of the statement. The issue also raises questions about the minister’s handling of the disclosure. By linking the suspected use of expired medicine to the investigation of Nipah deaths before the expert panel has established the facts, the government risks creating public alarm while the evidence remains under examination. At the same time, the LDF has an obvious political interest in defending the record of its previous administration. The opposition has accused the minister of damaging public confidence in Kerala’s public healthcare system and demanded an apology. Former two time chief minister and Leader of Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan of the CPI (M) has also urged the Chief Minister V D Satheesan of the Congress to intervene, alleging that the controversy is being used to divert attention from other administrative issues. The government, however, will have to answer a basic question regardless of the political exchange: How did hospital records come to indicate that vials purchased in 2021 and carrying an expiry date of May 2023 were used in later financial years? Keralam’s Nipah Response Kerala’s response to Nipah has received considerable national and international attention since the first outbreak in 2018 (Special arrangement) Kerala’s handling of Nipah has evolved through successive outbreaks under both the LDF administrations led by Pinarayi Vijayan. The first major outbreak in 2018, when K K Shailaja was Health Minister, tested the state’s surveillance, clinical management and contact-tracing systems. The subsequent outbreaks under Veena saw the health department build on those protocols through expanded testing, dedicated teams, isolation facilities and coordinated surveillance. The 2018 response involved extensive contact tracing and strengthened hospital and community surveillance. In 2019, a Nipah case was detected in Ernakulam, but no further spread was reported. A single case was reported in 2021. During the 2023 outbreak, the state activated a 19-team response structure, established a control room and expanded contact tracing and testing. In 2024, the health department intensified surveillance and monitoring during the Malappuram outbreak, while special fever clinics and dedicated response teams were deployed. These efforts have helped establish Kerala’s experience in managing recurrent Nipah threats as an important public-health case study. However, the current controversy shifts the focus from outbreak containment to the less visible but equally important aspects of healthcare administration: procurement, inventory management, drug expiry monitoring and accountability. news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月,喀拉拉邦卫生部长 K Muraleedharan 对 2023 年至 2025 年间向科泽科德医学院的尼帕患者服用的瑞德西韦小瓶可能过期表示担忧,引发了一场政治争议。部长的披露引发了对该州医疗保健管理部门的审查,前卫生部长维娜·乔治和医疗专业人士对过期药物与所提到的六例尼帕死亡之间的联系提出了质疑。政府已下令医疗委员会进行调查,以确定是否使用了过期的小瓶,是否将其提供给尼帕患者,以及是否对 治疗 结果产生任何影响。此次调查预计将澄清药品批次的过期状态以及服用这些药品的患者。这场争议凸显了药品采购和库存管理在公共卫生系统中的重要性,以及此类问题的政治影响。喀拉拉邦的尼帕应对措施曾因协调而受到赞扬,但现在因行政失误而受到审查。喀拉拉邦首次发生重大尼帕 暴发 事件发生于 2018 年,随后的 暴发 事件分别于 2019 年、2021 年、2023 年和 2024 年发生,每次事件均采用改进的协议进行管理。目前的情况引发了人们对医院记录的可靠性以及治疗中过期药物的潜在风险的质疑。

Share × Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Reddit Comments 0% Follow Us Thiruvananthapuram: The Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) will conduct an internal inquiry into the use of Remdesivir manufactured by US pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences in the treatment of Nipah patients, following questions over its procurement and supply. According to the register maintained by the Kozhikode Medical College, 690 vials of Gilead's Remdesivir were received on January 1, 2022. Of these, 10 vials were administered to Nipah patients on September 13, 2023. Another 256 vials were subsequently supplied to patients in different phases. However, records detailing from whom the medicine was procured, the quantity purchased and when it reached KMSCL have not been found. Officials said records relating to other medicines and medical equipment procured during the same period were available. The vials were labelled for clinical trial use only. Such vials are required to carry details of the patient receiving the drug, the prescribing doctor's name and the treatment protocol followed. The manufacturing date was not mentioned on the vials, although their expiry date was listed as September 2025. Remdesivir is the name of the antiviral drug molecule. The vials received in Kerala carried only the molecule's name and did not mention a brand name. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had approved Gilead's Remdesivir under the brand name Veklury on October 22, 2020, nearly two years before the vials reached Kerala. There had been speculation that the medicine was procured by the Central government through Hindustan Lifecare Limited (HLL) during the COVID pandemic and subsequently supplied to KMSCL. However, HLL officials have clarified that the company did not procure or supply Gilead's Remdesivir. ADVERTISEMENT CAG flags expired medicines in hospitals Meanwhile, a report by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has flagged instances of expired medicines being administered to patients in several hospitals across Kerala. The findings were based on an analysis of data from 2016-17 to 2021-22 covering 26 hospitals. Expired medicines were found to have been issued to hospital wards on 60 occasions, with the total value estimated at ₹89 lakh, according to the report released last year. The CAG observed that changes in the chemical composition of medicines after their expiry could pose serious risks to patients, potentially endangering their lives. Political reactions CPM Central Committee member and former health minister K K Shailaja dismissed allegations that expired medicines had been administered to Nipah patients. "The allegations that expired medicines were given to Nipah patients are baseless. Such claims are being made to cover up the current mismanagement in the Health Department," she said. Health Minister K Muraleedharan said he was willing to face a breach of privilege notice if he had misled the Assembly. "If I have misled the Assembly, let them move a breach of privilege notice. Experts will investigate the matter. If the medicines had expired, action will be taken," he said. Share × Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Reddit Comments 0% Follow Us Thiruvananthapuram: The Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) will conduct an internal inquiry into the use of Remdesivir manufactured by US pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences in the treatment of Nipah patients, following questions over its procurement and supply. According to the register maintained by the Kozhikode Medical College, 690 vials of Gilead's Remdesivir were received on January 1, 2022. Of these, 10 vials were administered to Nipah patients on September 13, 2023. Another 256 vials were subsequently supplied to patients in different phases. However, records detailing from whom the medicine was procured, the quantity purchased and when it reached KMSCL have not been found. Officials said records relating to other medicines and medical equipment procured during the same period were available. The vials were labelled for clinical trial use only. Such vials are required to carry details of the patient receiving the drug, the prescribing doctor's name and the treatment protocol followed. The manufacturing date was not mentioned on the vials, although their expiry date was listed as September 2025. Remdesivir is the name of the antiviral drug molecule. The vials received in Kerala carried only the molecule's name and did not mention a brand name. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had approved Gilead's Remdesivir under the brand name Veklury on October 22, 2020, nearly two years before the vials reached Kerala. There had been speculation that the medicine was procured by the Central government through Hindustan Lifecare Limited (HLL) during the COVID pandemic and subsequently supplied to KMSCL. However, HLL officials have clarified that the company did not procure or supply Gilead's Remdesivir. ADVERTISEMENT CAG flags expired medicines in hospitals Meanwhile, a report by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has flagged instances of expired medicines being administered to patients in several hospitals across Kerala. The findings were based on an analysis of data from 2016-17 to 2021-22 covering 26 hospitals. Expired medicines were found to have been issued to hospital wards on 60 occasions, with the total value estimated at ₹89 lakh, according to the report released last year. The CAG observed that changes in the chemical composition of medicines after their expiry could pose serious risks to patients, potentially endangering their lives. Political reactions CPM Central Committee member and former health minister K K Shailaja dismissed allegations that expired medicines had been administered to Nipah patients. "The allegations that expired medicines were given to Nipah patients are baseless. Such claims are being made to cover up the current mismanagement in the Health Department," she said. Health Minister K Muraleedharan said he was willing to face a breach of privilege notice if he had misled the Assembly. "If I have misled the Assembly, let them move a breach of privilege notice. Experts will investigate the matter. If the medicines had expired, action will be taken," he said. news.content: Dinamani Kannada Prabha Samakalika Malayalam Cinema Express Indulgexpress Edexlive Nov 03, 2026 2:29 AM Subscribe E-PAPER INDIA WORLD STATES CITIES OPINION EXPLAINER BUSINESS SPORTS GOOD NEWS ENTERTAINMENT VIDEOS LIVE BLOG INDIA WORLD STATES CITIES OPINION EXPLAINER BUSINESS SPORTS GOOD NEWS ENTERTAINMENT VIDEOS LIVE BLOG Trending Links Cyclone Murasu Bay of Bengal INDIA bloc rally November 1 INDIA bloc rally CJP Advertisement Keralam Kerala Nipah medicine row: CAG report, missing manufacturing dates come under scrutiny Congress leader Mathew Kuzhalnadan has pointed out that the CAG report had also made observations regarding allegations of expired medicines being used. Representative image(Express Illustrations) Pooja Nair Updated on: 31 Oct 2026, 3:08 am 3 min read Copied KOZHIKODE: Keralam’s hard-earned reputation for containing Nipah outbreaks is now facing an uncomfortable test, with allegations of expired medicines being administered to patients triggering questions over hospital procedures, drug safety and administrative accountability. As political accusations intensify, health experts say the focus must remain on establishing facts rather than allowing the controversy to undermine public confidence in the healthcare system. Congress leader Mathew Kuzhalnadan has pointed out that the CAG report had also made observations regarding allegations of expired medicines being used. “Based on the CAG report and the information my team gathered, we enquired. That’s when we came across the suspicion that Remdesivir was administered as one of the medicines for Nipah. A further probe revealed that vials without manufacturing dates are still with the Kozhikode medical college. That’s why the issue was raised in the assembly,” Kuzhalnadan told TNIE. In a Facebook post, Leader of Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan described the allegation that expired Remdesivir had been administered to Nipah patients as “a blatant lie”. He claimed that none of the six who died out of 13 Nipah patients during 2023-25 had received the drug from the medical college. “It is surprising that the health minister is taking the lead in spreading allegations and weakening the strength of the healthcare sector. His statements insult the dedication and sacrifices of healthcare workers, including Sister Lini,” Pinarayi, the then CM, said. He asked whether the controversy was intended to create an opportunity for private hospital lobbies. Meanwhile, experts have called for a scrutiny of the drug management system in the state. Amar Fettle, state nodal officer for adolescent health, said the pharmaceutical sector in a properly functioning government healthcare system was expected to be strictly regulated, with detailed records maintained whenever medicines were received, stored and issued. “In a normal government system, particularly in the pharmaceutical sector, there are established regulations. However, if officials concerned are reporting that the manufacturing date is missing, it needs to be taken seriously,” he said. At the same time, he cautioned against attributing Nipah deaths to the alleged use of expired medicines without scientific evidence. “Claiming that the deaths of Nipah patients were caused by the use of expired drugs is an extreme assumption. Nipah is an extremely dangerous and fatal virus that we have experienced in the recent past, and there have been several examples of its severity. Even the drugs administered now are not fully established as effective treatments. Therefore, blaming a particular drug itself is unacceptable without proper evidence,” he said. In a similar vein, V Ramankutty, a health economist, epidemiologist and academic associated with the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology), Thiruvananthapuram, said the focus should extend beyond the immediate controversy to the larger questions surrounding Keralam’s recurring Nipah outbreaks. None of the Nipah victims in Kerala received Remdesivir, says specialist doctor How NIPAH drug row unfolded June 3, 2021: Kerala Medical Services Corporation procures 3,000 vials of Remdesivir through Karunya scheme for J42 lakh. Stock reportedly carried an expiry date of May 30, 2023. Records at Kozhikode Government Medical College Hospital indicate that 102 vials were used in 2023-24, 34 in 2024-25 and 10 in 2025-26. Suspicions come up whether expired medicines were administered to patients C&AG report makes a remark about allegations over expired medicines. October 29, 2026: Issue reaches assembly as Congress leader Mathew Kuzhalnadan moves a submission. Health Minister K Muraleedharan expresses suspicion whether expired medicines were administered to deceased patients in 2023, 2024, 2025. Minister flags possible lapses as he said available records suggest that expired Remdesivir might have been administered at Kozhikode MCH. Minister says according to the hospital superintendent, the medicine’s packaging carried an expiry date but no manufacturing date. Says some stock was labelled ‘For clinical trial use’. Govt announces probe by a medical board headed by Dr R Aravind, head of Infectious Diseases Department at Thiruvananthapuram Medical College Hospital Critical care specialist Dr A S Anoop Kumar says none of the six Nipah fatalities between 2023 and 2025 received Remdesivir from Kozhikode Medical College. All deceased were diagnosed with Nipah after death. Anoop Kumar questions the department’s claim; asks why medicines past expiry date were still in its possession; asks for evidence to show they were administered to Nipah patients. Former health minister Veena George rubbishes allegations; says treatment details of Nipah patients were documented; says patients who received Remdesivir during 2023-25 at Kozhikode Medical College recovered. Former health minister K K Shailaja defends previous government; terms allegations unfounded; adds Remdesivir had been part of treatment efforts October 30, 2026: Minister says the government will wait for the expert committee’s findings before deciding on further action. What is to be probed? analysis.location_and_population: Kozhikode, Kerala, India. The Kozhikode Government Medical College Hospital and the state's healthcare system are involved. Nipah virus outbreaks in Kerala between 2023 and 2025 are referenced.
analysis.event: Allegations of expired medicines, specifically Remdesivir, being administered to Nipah patients have been raised, with the CAG report and hospital records under scrutiny. The issue was brought up in the assembly by Congress leader Mathew Kuzhalnadan, and the health minister expressed suspicion over the administration of expired drugs.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The controversy involves the potential administration of expired medicines to Nipah patients, raising concerns about drug safety and hospital procedures. However, no confirmed cases of expired drug use or adverse effects are reported. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the focus is on administrative accountability and maintaining public confidence in the healthcare system.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Kerala government has announced a probe by a medical board headed by Dr R Aravind. The health minister stated that the government will wait for the expert committee’s findings before deciding on further action. The issue remains under investigation, with no conclusive evidence yet.

analysis.brief_en: The New Indian Express reports on a controversy in Kerala, India, regarding the administration of expired medicines, particularly Remdesivir, to Nipah virus patients. The issue was raised in the assembly by Congress leader Mathew Kuzhalnadan, citing the CAG report and hospital records. Health Minister K Muraleedharan expressed suspicion about expired drug use, noting that some vials lacked manufacturing dates. A medical board will investigate the allegations, with the government awaiting expert findings before taking further action. Specialist doctors and health experts have called for scrutiny of the drug management system, emphasizing the need for scientific evidence before attributing Nipah deaths to expired medicines. The controversy highlights concerns about administrative accountability and public confidence in the healthcare system, though no confirmed cases of expired drug use or adverse effects have been reported.

India Nipah medicine row: Action after receiving expert panel report, says Keralam Health Minister PTI 30 October, 2026 11:45 am IST Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Follow Us : Text Size: A- A+ Kozhikode (Keralam), Oct 30 (PTI) Health Minister K Muraleedharan on Friday said the government would take further action after receiving a report from an expert committee probing the allegations that expired doses of Remdesivir were administered to Nipah patients in Keralam in previous years. In a reply to a submission by Congress MLA Mathew Kuzhalnadan in the Assembly, the minister had said that Remdesivir procured in 2021 had an expiry date of May 2023 but might have been administered to patients admitted to Kozhikode Medical College till 2025. Speaking to reporters here, Muraleedharan said the information presented to the Assembly was based on reports from responsible officials of the Health Department and that he would not make further comments until the expert committee submitted its findings. Show Full Article The government would investigate whether the deaths of Nipah patients were linked to the administration of expired medicine and whether other patients who received the drug had suffered any adverse effects, Muraleedharan said. “There are several doubts regarding the medicine, including whether it was administered after its expiry date. We will investigate and take a decision,” he said. The minister clarified that there were no concerns about the quality or efficacy of Remdesivir itself and that the issue under investigation was whether expired doses had been administered to patients. Recalling the procurement of the drug during the Nipah outbreak after the UDF government came to power, he said efforts to source it from different parts of the country had failed as the available stocks in Mumbai had expired. Subsequently, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) informed the government that the medicine was available in Bahrain, following which it was procured within 48 hours, he said. He said patients who received the medicine within its validity period had recovered and asserted that the controversy concerned its expiry date rather than the drug’s efficacy. Muraleedharan said the expert committee headed by Dr Aravind would conduct an impartial examination without any preconceived conclusions. The probe would also examine how the medicine was procured and supplied, the role of intermediaries and the functioning of KMSCL. The government would investigate whether any agents were involved in the procurement process, he said. The minister also said the Kozhikode Medical College superintendent had informed him that the packaging of the Remdesivir medicine listed an expiry date but did not mention its manufacturing date. Both details were normally required on medicine packaging, and the discrepancy would be examined, he said. He said the government would also examine information that the medicine supplied to patients was labelled for clinical trial use, adding that he had not received an authoritative report confirming all the details. “Further decisions on the issues would be taken after receiving the expert committee’s findings,” he said. He also referred to concerns about the involvement of foreign pharmaceutical companies in the state’s medicine procurement, saying the government would examine the related transactions and procedures. It was on Thursday that Muraleedharan replied to the submission at the Assembly. The minister said that KMSCL had last procured 3,000 vials of Remdesivir through its Karunya scheme on June 3, 2021, at Rs 42 lakh. The medicine had an expiry date of May 30, 2023. According to a report received from Kozhikode Medical College Hospital, 102 vials of Remdesivir were used during 2023-24, 34 during 2024-25, 10 during 2025-26 and 50 during 2026-27. However, the 50 vials used during 2026-27 had been procured from Bahrain on June 12, 2026, for treating a Nipah patient, the minister said. In view of these details, there was a suspicion that Remdesivir administered to patients at the medical college during 2023, 2024 and 2025 had expired, he said. The minister said instructions had been issued to the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) and the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) to collect details of all patients who had similarly received Remdesivir from health institutions. He said six Nipah cases were reported in 2023, of whom two died. In 2024, two cases were reported, and both patients died, while two of the three Nipah patients reported in 2025 also succumbed to the infection. One Nipah case was reported in 2026, and the patient recovered. Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus that can be transmitted between animals and humans. Fruit bats, also known as flying foxes, are the natural reservoir of the Nipah virus. The virus can also cause illness in pigs and humans. news.title_zh: 尼帕医药行:喀拉拉邦卫生部长表示,收到专家小组报告后采取行动 - ThePrint
news.source_body_en: The Kerala Health Minister, K Muraleedharan, announced on October 30, 2026, that the government would investigate whether expired doses of Remdesivir were administered to Nipah patients in Keralam during previous years. The expert committee, led by Dr Aravind, will conduct an impartial examination of the issue. The minister clarified that the concern is specifically about the expiry date of the drug, not its quality or efficacy. He mentioned that the KMSCL procured the medicine from Bahrain in June 2026, and there were discrepancies in the packaging details. The report also noted that six Nipah cases were reported in 2023, with two deaths; two cases in 2024, both resulting in deaths; two of three cases in 2025 also succumbing to the infection; and one case in 2026 that recovered. The government is collecting details of all patients who received Remdesivir from health institutions. The investigation will also examine the procurement process, the role of intermediaries, and the functioning of KMSCL. The minister emphasized that further decisions will be made only after the expert committee’s findings are received.
news.content_zh: 喀拉拉邦卫生部长 K Muraleedharan 于 2026 年 10 月 30 日宣布,政府将调查前几年是否向喀拉拉邦的尼帕患者服用过期剂量的瑞德西韦。由阿拉文德博士领导的专家委员会将对这一问题进行公正的审查。部长澄清说,人们特别担心的是药物的有效期,而不是其质量或功效。他提到,KMSCL于2026年6月从巴林采购该药品,包装细节存在差异。报告还指出,2023 年报告了 6 起尼帕病例,其中两人死亡;2024 年发生两例,均导致死亡;2025 年,三分之二的病例也会死于感染;2026 年有 1 例康复。政府正在从医疗机构收集所有接受瑞德西韦治疗的患者的详细信息。调查还将审查采购流程、中介机构的作用以及 KMSCL 的运作情况。部长强调,只有在收到专家委员会的调查结果后才会做出进一步的决定。

Hunting Invisible Viruses: Threats to Humans Lurking in the Animal Kingdom Home / All News / SPECTRUM. Hunting Invisible Viruses: Threats to Humans Lurking in the Animal Kingdom 29 October 2026 Sonata Kuncė SPECTRUM. Hunting Invisible Viruses: Threats to Humans Lurking in the Animal Kingdom ResearchSpectrum JournalVU News Illustration by Marija Benetytė Viruses are the most abundant biological entities on Earth. Scientists estimate that more than 99% of them remain undescribed. Some of these invisible pathogens live in wild animals, and often neither cause serious illness nor pose a major threat to humans. Occasionally, however, viruses cross the species barrier and give rise to new diseases. One such example is the Nipah virus outbreak in Malaysia. The virus passed from fruit bats to pigs and subsequently infected humans, claiming more than 100 lives. To understand how such viruses emerge and evolve, Dr Milda Norkienė, a researcher at the Life Sciences Center of Vilnius University, and her colleagues are studying the diversity and evolution of polyomaviruses found in animals, as well as their potential threat to human health. Viruses that live among us Viruses are often associated with disease, but most of them are not actually dangerous to humans. ‘There is an enormous diversity of viruses in nature, and we encounter them constantly without even noticing. For example, when we eat plants, we also ingest plant viruses, while the bacteria living in our gut are infected by viruses of their own – bacteriophages. Yet this doesn’t mean that all of them are dangerous to us. Most are highly ‘selective’ and can reproduce only in a particular host,’ said VU researcher Dr Norkienė. The same is true of polyomaviruses. Many of us were probably infected with at least one of them in childhood without ever realising it, as the infection usually causes no symptoms. These viruses can remain in the body for many years and become active only under exceptional circumstances. Although the polyomavirus family is relatively small, research into these viruses has profoundly influenced biology and medicine. By analysing how they take over cellular machinery and force cells to copy viral genetic material, researchers have gained a better understanding of cell division, DNA replication, and even the development of certain tumours. This is why the search for new polyomaviruses continues to this day. ‘Polyomaviruses are found in a wide range of animals, from mammals to fish. Although few people have heard of them, scientists have already identified 16 polyomavirus species associated with humans, most of them only in the past two decades,’ explained Dr Norkienė, whose research focuses on these viruses. Most of these viruses are harmless to humans. However, when the immune system is weakened or a person is taking immunosuppressive medication, some polyomaviruses can reactivate and cause serious health problems. For instance, the BK virus is one of the polyomaviruses found in humans. Most people become infected with it in childhood, but the infection generally produces no symptoms. Following a kidney transplant, however, the virus can cause inflammation and damage the transplanted organ. The Merkel cell polyomavirus, meanwhile, is associated with a rare but highly aggressive form of skin cancer. Thus, it is important for researchers not only to discover new viruses but also to understand the circumstances under which they become dangerous. Discovering a new virus from a barely visible trace When we think of new virus discoveries, we tend to picture sophisticated laboratory equipment or major scientific breakthroughs. Yet the first step is often far less spectacular. It usually begins in the laboratory, with researchers analysing animal samples. The first indication of a potentially new virus may be nothing more than a barely visible DNA band on a gel. At first glance, such a band may seem unremarkable, but it can provide the first clue to a previously unknown virus. When examining animal samples, researchers look for genetic traces of viruses. Any positive result from an animal species that has not previously been studied immediately raises a question: is this a known virus, or something that no one has ever described before? This is where the real detective work begins. DNA gel electrophoresis. The first lane on the left contains a DNA size marker; the second shows a positive signal – a DNA fragment; while the third and fourth show negative results. Photo credit: doctoral researcher Monika Repšytė. ‘Is it really a virus? Could it be laboratory contamination? Does the virus actually live in this animal?’ These are just some of the questions that researchers must answer. They reconstruct the virus’s entire genetic sequence, compare it with data stored in international databases, and check whether the same virus has ever been detected before. A single finding is generally not enough: researchers need to establish that it is not merely a chance occurrence. That is why they need to detect a similar virus in more than one animal of the same species and, ideally, across different geographical locations. Even then, however, there are usually more questions than answers. One of the most important is whether the scientists have identified a genuinely new virus or simply one that had previously gone unnoticed. New or just newly discovered? News of a newly discovered virus often sounds alarming. However, ‘new’ does not necessarily mean ‘recently emerged’. More often, it means something quite different: researchers have detected and comprehensively described the virus for the first time. In fact, most viruses being discovered today are not new to nature – they are new only to science. Many of the polyomaviruses now being identified in animals have probably been around for thousands, if not millions, of years, but have simply never been studied before. Nevertheless, new discoveries sometimes raise more complex questions. If a virus causes unusually severe disease in its host, researchers begin to consider whether it has truly been adapted to that species for a long time. In such cases, they seek to answer one crucial question: could the virus have recently crossed over into a new host? A European hamster in its natural habitat Could a virus cross the species barrier? ‘Our immune system has evolved to cope with constant exposure to viruses, but sometimes the slightest vulnerability is all a virus needs. Some viruses become a threat when they cross the species barrier – that is, when they are transmitted from animals to humans. The diseases they cause are known as zoonoses. Others, including polyomaviruses, are often already present in our bodies and may lie dormant and undetected for years, until a weakened immune system gives them an opportunity to reactivate and cause disease,’ explained VU researcher Dr Norkienė. More than 70% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonoses – diseases caused by pathogens transmitted from animals. This is why virologists ask not only ‘What virus have we found?’ but also ‘Could it adapt to a new host?’ How, then, can scientists test something that has not yet occurred in nature? To do so, they use pseudoviruses – safe surrogates that mimic real viruses. Their viral genetic material is replaced with a fluorescent marker, which means that they cannot replicate or cause disease, even though their outer structure resembles that of a real virus. If a pseudovirus enters a cell, researchers can detect it using a specialised microscope. In other words, they can observe the initial interactions between the virus and the cell and safely investigate whether the virus could theoretically take the first step towards infecting a new host. Of course, this does not necessarily mean that the virus will infect a new species in nature. Many factors influence whether this happens – from the host’s immune system to environmental conditions. Such experiments can nevertheless provide initial evidence for or against the hypothesis that a virus may be capable of adapting to a new host. The multifunctional Agno protein of a rodent polyomavirus is shown in green within the host cell; cell nuclei are stained blue and cell membranes red. Photo credit: Emilija Vasiliūnaitė. The specific antibodies used in this study were developed at the Department of Immunology of the Life Sciences Center, Vilnius University Experiments of this kind help scientists better understand how viruses recognise cells and which factors determine their ability to infect different hosts. Although this technology remains relatively uncommon worldwide, Vilnius University researchers are among those using polyomavirus pseudoviruses in their studies. In collaboration with Dr Christopher B. Buck, a virologist at the US National Cancer Institute, they have developed a rodent polyomavirus pseudovirus technology, enabling safe investigation of how viruses might adapt to new hosts. When even brewer’s yeast can recognise a viral protein Sometimes the most fascinating discoveries emerge where they are least expected: during one experiment, researchers found that the major capsid protein of a polyomavirus triggered a strong stress response even in brewer’s yeast. Brewer’s yeast is one of the simplest eukaryotic organisms, therefore, the finding was particularly surprising. As the yeast cells synthesised the polyomavirus protein, they began to cluster into clumps visible to the naked eye – a mechanism that helps them protect themselves against adverse conditions. Flocculating yeast. Photo credit: Dr Milda Norkienė. ‘Even yeast cells can recognise that a viral protein may be pathogenic and send a warning signal to surrounding cells; thus, we had to work out how to switch off that signal,’ said Dr Norkienė. Such unexpected observations shed light on how viruses affect living cells and why some of them are so successful at adapting to very different organisms. Why look for these viruses now? The search for new viruses is driven by more than scientific curiosity. Climate change, human mobility, growing contact between animals and humans, changing ecosystems, and the increasing number of people with impaired immune systems are all creating new opportunities for viruses to spread. The more we know today about the viruses circulating in nature, the better prepared we will be to face tomorrow’s challenges. The Vilnius University polyomavirus research group, funded by the Research Council of Lithuania, has already identified several new polyomaviruses that infect animals, although none have been found to pose a threat to humans. Most viruses discovered today are unlikely ever to harm us. Yet this is precisely why it is important to study them before they ever have the chance to become a threat. Scientists do not know how many such viruses remain hidden in nature. However, each new discovery brings us closer to understanding the invisible world that surrounds us. Share FacebookLinkedInX

This is where the real detective work begins. DNA gel electrophoresis. The first lane on the left contains a DNA size marker; the second shows a positive signal – a DNA fragment; while the third and fourth show negative results. Photo credit: doctoral researcher Monika Repšytė. ‘Is it really a virus? Could it be laboratory contamination? Does the virus actually live in this animal?’ These are just some of the questions that researchers must answer. They reconstruct the virus’s entire genetic sequence, compare it with data stored in international databases, and check whether the same virus has ever been detected before. A single finding is generally not enough: researchers need to establish that it is not merely a chance occurrence. That is why they need to detect a similar virus in more than one animal of the same species and, ideally, across different geographical locations. Even then, however, there are usually more questions than answers. One of the most important is whether the scientists have identified a genuinely new virus or simply one that had previously gone unnoticed. New or just newly discovered? News of a newly discovered virus often sounds alarming. However, ‘new’ does not necessarily mean ‘recently emerged’. More often, it means something quite different: researchers have detected and comprehensively described the virus for the first time. In fact, most viruses being discovered today are not new to nature – they are new only to science. Many of the polyomaviruses now being identified in animals have probably been around for thousands, if not millions, of years, but have simply never been studied before. Nevertheless, new discoveries sometimes raise more complex questions. If a virus causes unusually severe disease in its host, researchers begin to consider whether it has truly been adapted to that species for a long time. In such cases, they seek to answer one crucial question: could the virus have recently crossed over into a new host? A European hamster in its natural habitat Could a virus cross the species barrier? ‘Our immune system has evolved to cope with constant exposure to viruses, but sometimes the slightest vulnerability is all a virus needs. Some viruses become a threat when they cross the species barrier – that is, when they are transmitted from animals to humans. The diseases they cause are known as zoonoses. Others, including polyomaviruses, are often already present in our bodies and may lie dormant and undetected for years, until a weakened immune system gives them an opportunity to reactivate and cause disease,’ explained VU researcher Dr Norkienė. More than 70% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonoses – diseases caused by pathogens transmitted from animals. This is why virologists ask not only ‘What virus have we found?’ but also ‘Could it adapt to a new host?’ How, then, can scientists test something that has not yet occurred in nature? To do so, they use pseudoviruses – safe surrogates that mimic real viruses. Their viral genetic material is replaced with a fluorescent marker, which means that they cannot replicate or cause disease, even though their outer structure resembles that of a real virus. If a pseudovirus enters a cell, researchers can detect it using a specialised microscope. In other words, they can observe the initial interactions between the virus and the cell and safely investigate whether the virus could theoretically take the first step towards infecting a new host. Of course, this does not necessarily mean that the virus will infect a new species in nature. Many factors influence whether this happens – from the host’s immune system to environmental conditions. Such experiments can nevertheless provide initial evidence for or against the hypothesis that a virus may be capable of adapting to a new host. The multifunctional Agno protein of a rodent polyomavirus is shown in green within the host cell; cell nuclei are stained blue and cell membranes red. Photo credit: Emilija Vasiliūnaitė. The specific antibodies used in this study were developed at the Department of Immunology of the Life Sciences Center, Vilnius University Experiments of this kind help scientists better understand how viruses recognise cells and which factors determine their ability to infect different hosts. Although this technology remains relatively uncommon worldwide, Vilnius University researchers are among those using polyomavirus pseudoviruses in their studies. In collaboration with Dr Christopher B. Buck, a virologist at the US National Cancer Institute, they have developed a rodent polyomavirus pseudovirus technology, enabling safe investigation of how viruses might adapt to new hosts. When even brewer’s yeast can recognise a viral protein Sometimes the most fascinating discoveries emerge where they are least expected: during one experiment, researchers found that the major capsid protein of a polyomavirus triggered a strong stress response even in brewer’s yeast. Brewer’s yeast is one of the simplest eukaryotic organisms, therefore, the finding was particularly surprising. As the yeast cells synthesised the polyomavirus protein, they began to cluster into clumps visible to the naked eye – a mechanism that helps them protect themselves against adverse conditions. Flocculating yeast. Photo credit: Dr Milda Norkienė. ‘Even yeast cells can recognise that a viral protein may be pathogenic and send a warning signal to surrounding cells; thus, we had to work out how to switch off that signal,’ said Dr Norkienė. Such unexpected observations shed light on how viruses affect living cells and why some of them are so successful at adapting to very different organisms. Why look for these viruses now? The search for new viruses is driven by more than scientific curiosity. Climate change, human mobility, growing contact between animals and humans, changing ecosystems, and the increasing number of people with impaired immune systems are all creating new opportunities for viruses to spread. The more we know today about the viruses circulating in nature, the better prepared we will be to face tomorrow’s challenges. The Vilnius University polyomavirus research group, funded by the Research Council of Lithuania, has already identified several new polyomaviruses that infect animals, although none have been found to pose a threat to humans. Most viruses discovered today are unlikely ever to harm us. Yet this is precisely why it is important to study them before they ever have the chance to become a threat. Scientists do not know how many such viruses remain hidden in nature. However, each new discovery brings us closer to understanding the invisible world that surrounds us. Share FacebookLinkedInX

news.content_zh: 维尔纽斯大学的这篇新闻报道重点介绍了多瘤病毒的研究,多瘤病毒是在包括人类在内的各种动物中发现的病毒家族。Milda Norkienė 博士和她的同事正在研究这些病毒,以了解它们引起健康问题的可能性,特别是当免疫系统受到损害时。报告指出,虽然大多数多瘤病毒是无害的,但有些在特定条件下可能变得危险。该研究涉及分析动物样本中病毒的遗传痕迹,第一步通常是检测凝胶上几乎不可见的 DNA 带。科学家必须确定该病毒是新病毒还是以前未被注意到的病毒,他们使用专门的方法来评估其对新 宿主 的适应性。这项研究是更好地了解病毒多样性及其对人类健康影响的持续努力的一部分。报告中没有提及具体的暴发或病例编号,但该研究旨在识别和表征可能对人类构成风险的新病毒。

Keralam govt orders probe TNN / Updated: Oct 30, 2026, 10:42 IST Save Comments Share Aa +Text Size Small Medium Large Print In Kerala, patients were administered remdesivir, an antiviral drug approved for treating Covid-19, despite its expiration THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Antiviral drug remdesivir, approved to treat Covid-19, was administered to patients, including those infected with Nipah virus, at Kozhikode govt medical college hospital in 2024 and 2025 from stock that expired in May 2023, health minister K Muraleedharan told the assembly on Thursday. Govt has ordered a detailed probe into the incident.Replying to a submission by Mathew Kuzhalnadan, Muraleedharan said a medical board headed by Dr Aravind Reghukumar, head of infectious diseases at govt medical college hospital, Thiruvananthapuram, would investigate whether the use of expired remdesivir had contributed to Nipah deaths or caused adverse effects in other patients.He said the directorate of medical education (DME) and the directorate of health services (DHS) had been directed to collect details of patients who received remdesivir during the period. The drug, administered through intravenous infusion, was supplied to healthcare institutions by Kerala Medical Services Corporation Ltd (KMSCL) to meet emergency treatment requirements.The medicine was last procured on June 3, 2021, through KMSCL’s Karunya division. The corporation bought 3,000 vials for Rs 42 lakh, with the stock expiring on May 30, 2023.A report from Kozhikode medical college hospital showed that 102 vials were used in 2023-24, 34 in 2024-25 and 10 in 2025-26. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like View Homes for Sale with AcreageHomes.com Undo Another 50 vials were recorded as used in 2026-27, but Muraleedharan said these had been brought from Bahrain on June 12, 2026, to treat a Nipah patient. The records have raised concerns that expired remdesivir may have been administered to patients between 2023 and 2025. Keralam govt orders probe TNN / Updated: Oct 30, 2026, 10:42 IST Save Comments Share Aa +Text Size Small Medium Large Print In Kerala, patients were administered remdesivir, an antiviral drug approved for treating Covid-19, despite its expiration THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Antiviral drug remdesivir, approved to treat Covid-19, was administered to patients, including those infected with Nipah virus, at Kozhikode govt medical college hospital in 2024 and 2025 from stock that expired in May 2023, health minister K Muraleedharan told the assembly on Thursday. Govt has ordered a detailed probe into the incident.Replying to a submission by Mathew Kuzhalnadan, Muraleedharan said a medical board headed by Dr Aravind Reghukumar, head of infectious diseases at govt medical college hospital, Thiruvananthapuram, would investigate whether the use of expired remdesivir had contributed to Nipah deaths or caused adverse effects in other patients.He said the directorate of medical education (DME) and the directorate of health services (DHS) had been directed to collect details of patients who received remdesivir during the period. The drug, administered through intravenous infusion, was supplied to healthcare institutions by Kerala Medical Services Corporation Ltd (KMSCL) to meet emergency treatment requirements.The medicine was last procured on June 3, 2021, through KMSCL’s Karunya division. The corporation bought 3,000 vials for Rs 42 lakh, with the stock expiring on May 30, 2023.A report from Kozhikode medical college hospital showed that 102 vials were used in 2023-24, 34 in 2024-25 and 10 in 2025-26. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like View Homes for Sale with AcreageHomes.com Undo Another 50 vials were recorded as used in 2026-27, but Muraleedharan said these had been brought from Bahrain on June 12, 2026, to treat a Nipah patient. The records have raised concerns that expired remdesivir may have been administered to patients between 2023 and 2025. Top News Audio Briefing - 03 Nov 2026 7 AM 0:00 5:53 Advertisement Citing the state’s Nipah figures, the minister said two of the six cases reported in 2023 were fatal. Both cases reported in 2024 resulted in deaths, while two of the three cases reported in 2025 were fatal. The sole case reported in 2026 recovered. news.source_body_en: The Kerala government has ordered an investigation into whether the use of expired remdesivir contributed to Nipah virus deaths. According to the health minister, expired drug stock was administered to patients, including those with Nipah virus, at Kozhikode and Thiruvananthapuram govt medical college hospitals between 2023 and 2025. The probe, led by Dr Aravind Reghukumar, aims to determine if the expired drug caused adverse effects or fatalities. Between 2023 and 2025, there were six Nipah cases, with two fatalities in 2023, two in 2024, and two in 2025. The sole case in 2026 recovered. The drug was supplied by Kerala Medical Services Corporation Ltd (KMSCL) and was last procured on June 3, 2021. The investigation is ongoing, and the government is collecting details of patients who received remdesivir during the period. The report highlights concerns about the potential risks of using expired antiviral drugs in treating Nipah virus patients.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, November 3, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Memory Effects and Optimal Control Reshape Nipah Virus Spillover in Fractional Multi-Host Model by October 29, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Memory Effects and Optimal Control Reshape Nipah Virus Spillover in Fractional Multi-Host Model Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Mathematicians have built a fractional-order epidemic model that tracks Nipah virus transmission simultaneously across human, pig, and bird populations, and paired it with an optimal control framework to identify the most effective intervention strategies. The study, published as open access research in Discover Analytics on 13 July 2026 by Sunday Oluwafemi Gbodogbe and Adedapo Chris Loyinmi, formulates the model using the Caputo fractional derivative, an operator that incorporates memory effects arising from past infection states, which classical integer-order models do not account for. The motivation rests on the epidemiology of Nipah virus, a zoonotic pathogen the World Health Organization has classified as a priority pathogen requiring urgent research attention. Bats of the genus Pteropus serve as the primary natural reservoir, pigs act as intermediate hosts, and humans acquire infection through contaminated fruit, exposure to bat saliva or urine, contact with infected pigs, or human-to-human transmission in healthcare and family settings. No approved vaccine or targeted antiviral treatment exists, and patient management relies primarily on supportive care, with antiviral agents such as ribavirin showing limited effectiveness. The model divides human and pig populations into susceptible, infected, treated, and recovered compartments, while the bird population is partitioned into susceptible and infected classes. Transmission occurs through standard-incidence forces of infection that explicitly represent cross-species pathways: birds transmit to pigs and humans, pigs transmit to humans and within their own population, and infected humans contribute to further human spread. Birds act as the primary reservoir in the model’s biological assumptions, pigs serve as intermediate hosts capable of passing infection to humans, and treatment reduces disease burden without conferring immediate immunity. The Caputo fractional derivative of order between zero and one introduces a memory kernel that allows past states to influence current dynamics, capturing effects such as cumulative exposure, delayed disease progression, and behavioral adaptation. A uniform fractional order is assumed across all compartments for analytical consistency. The authors establish that solutions remain nonnegative and bounded within a biologically feasible region, prove existence and uniqueness of solutions via a fixed-point argument, and derive the disease-free equilibrium where all infected and treated compartments vanish. Using the next-generation matrix method, the team computed the basic reproduction number as the maximum of three host-specific thresholds, one each for humans, pigs, and birds. Because the underlying matrix is upper triangular, its eigenvalues fall on the diagonal, yielding a closed-form expression in which transmission coefficients and contact modification parameters appear in the numerator and treatment, natural mortality, and disease-induced mortality rates in the denominator. Sensitivity analysis shows that transmission rates and contact modification parameters carry positive sensitivity indices of one, making them the dominant drivers of disease spread, while treatment and removal rates reduce transmission. The stability analysis follows the fractional-order criterion that an equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable only when every eigenvalue of the linearized system satisfies an argument condition tied to the fractional order. The disease-free equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable when the reproduction number is below one and unstable when it exceeds one, with a Lyapunov-based argument extending this to global stability within the feasible region. When the reproduction number surpasses one, the authors show that a unique endemic equilibrium exists and can be locally stable under the same eigenvalue condition. Numerical simulations using a predictor-corrector Adams-Bashforth-Moulton scheme with a time step of 0.1 reveal a striking role for memory. Across scenarios testing fractional orders of 0.8, 0.9, and the classical integer-order case of 1, decreasing the fractional order significantly delayed epidemic peaks and prolonged infection duration, with the strongest sensitivity appearing in the human and pig populations. The abstract reports that reducing the fractional order lowered peak infection levels by more than 40 percent in some scenarios, while the classical case exhibited faster epidemic growth and quicker decay. The bird population showed monotone decline across all orders, though with markedly slower decline for smaller fractional values. The optimal control framework introduces four time-dependent interventions bounded between zero and one: preventive measures reducing transmission to humans, intensified treatment for infected humans, biosecurity measures in pigs, and intensified treatment for infected pigs. Applying Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle yields a Hamiltonian, an adjoint system, and explicit characterizations of the optimal controls in terms of costate variables and infection forces. The objective functional balances the epidemiological burden of infection in each host population against quadratic costs of implementing each control. The simulation results carry a consistent practical message. Under optimal control, infected human and pig populations rapidly decline to near-zero levels in both disease-free and endemic settings, whereas uncontrolled dynamics show pronounced epidemic peaks followed by slow decay. Susceptible human and pig populations are better preserved under control, treated compartments attain substantially lower peaks, and phase portraits show controlled trajectories contracting toward the disease-free equilibrium while uncontrolled trajectories exhibit large persistent excursions. The optimal controls are strongest at early times and decrease thereafter, a front-loaded structure the authors interpret as evidence that early aggressive intervention is most effective. The authors frame the work as filling a gap in which existing models either focused on single-host dynamics without memory effects or applied fractional-order models to single populations without cross-species spillover mechanisms. They caution that the model is general rather than fitted to specific outbreak data: parameter values are taken from existing literature on Nipah virus dynamics or chosen to be biologically reasonable where empirical estimates are unavailable, no empirical datasets were generated or analyzed, and future work is expected to incorporate spatial heterogeneity, stochastic effects, and data-driven parameter estimation. Within those limits, the study argues that memory effects and coordinated, early interventions targeting both human and animal populations jointly shape whether a zoonotic spillover event fades out or persists.
